title: Multitrait GWAS and functional validation reveal genetic loci for gastric cancer

paper_content.abstract: Gastric cancer is a leading cause of cancer-related death, particularly in East Asia, yet its genetic basis remains incompletely understood. Using genome-wide association study data from BioBank Japan, we show that gastric cancer shares significant genetic associations with 25 other phenotypes, most notably cardiovascular conditions such as angina pectoris and myocardial infarction. Mendelian randomization supports a causal role of these traits in gastric cancer risk. Multitrait analysis of GWAS reveals a novel pleiotropic locus at 12q22 (rs12814712) that is shared between gastric cancer and cardiovascular traits. Functional experiments demonstrate that the risk allele at this locus reduces transcriptional activity and downregulates the expression of nearby genes, particularly VEZT. In gastric cancer cells, overexpression of VEZT and NR2C1 suppress proliferation and migration, whereas their knockdown promotes malignancy. Our analysis identifies rs12814712 as a novel susceptibility locus for gastric cancer and underscores its regulatory role in disease-related gene networks.
paper_content.introduction:
According to global cancer statistics for 2022, gastric cancer ranks fifth in terms of both incidence and mortality worldwide, accounting for 968,350 new cases and 659,853 deaths, respectively 1. The incidence of gastric cancer varies regionally, with higher rates in East Asia and Eastern Europe and lower rates in Northern Europe and North America 1, which are likely influenced by environmental, lifestyle, and genetic factors. Empirical studies have shown that gastric cancer is the result of a complex interaction of genetic and environmental risk factors 2. Risk factors encompass a spectrum ranging from Helicobacter pylori (HP) infection to dietary habits such as the consumption of pickled foods, as well as behaviours such as alcohol consumption and tobacco use. Among these, HP infection emerges as the most influential determinant. Moreover, genetic studies, including twin and genome-wide association studies (GWASs), have revealed a substantial genetic contribution to gastric cancer susceptibility, with heritability estimates of approximately 20.9% in the Chinese population and 22% in Nordic twins 3,4.

Gastric cancer displays substantial polygenicity, with East Asian populations showing the identification of at least 15 risk loci through GWAS. For instance, in a two-stage GWAS in Japan, a notable association was found between an intronic SNP (rs2976392) within the PSCA gene and diffuse-type gastric cancer 5. Similarly, researchers at Nanjing Medical University reported genetic variations at loci 1p35.2 and 6p22.1 in the Chinese population, which correlated with increased gastric cancer risk 6. Moreover, they elucidated the roles of PRKAA1 at the 5p13.1 locus and NOC3L at the 10q23.33 locus in gastric tumour pathogenesis 7. In contrast, only the 11q22.3 locus was identified in Europeans 8. Furthermore, several genes within these risk loci, such as MUC1 (1q22), SPOCD1 (1p35.2), PSCA (8q24.3), PRKAA1 (5p13.1), BTN3A2 (6p22.1), and NOC3L (10q23.33), have been functionally validated as susceptibility genes for gastric cancer 5-7,9.

Recent advances in statistical methodologies for GWAS analyses have made it possible to conduct joint analyses of traits that share genetic architecture 10. Through meta-analyses of GWAS summary statistics for genetically correlated traits, multitrait analysis of GWAS (MTAG) not only enhances statistical power but also identifies pleiotropic genetic variants that influence interconnected traits. This cross-trait analysis approach has proven successful in numerous cancer research studies. Additionally, it has been applied to the investigation of seven upper gastrointestinal disorders 11. However, to the best of our knowledge, no multitrait GWAS analysis specifically targeting gastric cancer has been conducted to date.

In this study, we identified multiple novel pleiotropic loci associated with gastric cancer using GWAS data from the BioBank Japan (BBJ) 12. Notably, we observed that several genes adjacent to these loci might be involved in gastric cancer pathogenesis, as documented in the literature. We collected gastric cancer samples and conducted functional experiments to elucidate the regulatory relationships between the identified loci and their neighbouring genes, as well as to explore the potential roles of candidate genes in the aetiology of gastric cancer.
paper_content.results:
In this study, we utilized GWAS data from BBJ and identified multiple new pleiotropic loci associated with gastric cancer using MTAG. Notably, we observed that several genes near the novel 12q22 locus might be involved in the pathogenesis of gastric cancer. Consequently, we collected clinical gastric cancer samples and conducted functional experiments to elucidate the potential regulatory relationships between the identified loci and their neighbouring genes and to explore the potential roles of candidate genes in the aetiology of gastric cancer. An overview of our study is provided in Fig. 1.

Genetic correlations between gastric cancer and associated phenotypes
We analysed GWAS data from BBJ to explore the genetic correlation between gastric cancer and 95 phenotypes, including diseases, biomarkers, and medication usage, in East Asians. Following multiple testing correction, our analysis revealed a significant positive genetic correlation between gastric cancer and 25 cardiovascular-related traits, including diseases like angina pectoris (AP, rg = 0.4611, PFDR = 0.0001), myocardial infarction (MI, rg = 0.3415, PFDR = 0.0009), blood pressure measurements such as diastolic blood pressure (DBP, rg = 0.2549, PFDR = 0.0028), systolic blood pressure (SBP, rg = 0.2421, PFDR = 0.001), and mean arterial pressure (MAP, rg = 0.2612, PFDR = 0.0009), as well as the use of cardiovascular drugs like calcium channel blockers (CCBUM, rg = 0.3561, PFDR = 4.56 × 10-7), renin-angiotensin system inhibitors (AARSUM, rg = 0.4309, PFDR = 1.41 × 10-8), HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors (HCRIUM, rg = 0.3786, PFDR = 1.82 × 10-6) and salicylic acid and derivatives (SADUM, rg = 0.4115, PFDR = 0.0002). Additionally, positive genetic correlations were identified between gastric cancer and other cancer types, including lung cancer (LC, rg = 0.7442, PFDR = 0.0058) and colorectal cancer (CRC, rg = 0.3043, PFDR = 0.002) (Supplementary Table S1, Fig. 2).

Causal Impact of Cardiovascular-Related Factors on Gastric Cancer
To further investigate the relationship between cardiovascular traits and gastric cancer, we conducted Mendelian randomization (MR) analysis. The inverse-variance weighted (IVW) method revealed that after false discovery rate (FDR) correction, eight cardiovascular-related factors were significantly associated with an increased risk of gastric cancer, including AP (OR 1.289, 95% CI 1.060–1.568; PFDR = 0.0192), stable angina pectoris (SAP, OR 1.408, 95% CI 1.243–1.596; PFDR = 5.56 × 10-7), and MI (OR 1.179, 95% CI 1.094–1.270; PFDR = 5.36 × 10-5). Additionally, antithrombotic agents (AAUM, OR 1.829; 95% CI 1.343-2.493; PFDR = 3.61 × 10-4), beta-blocking agents (BBAUM, OR 1.478, 95% CI 1.108-1.972; PFDR = 0.0159), SADUM (OR 1.799, 95% CI 1.412-2.293; PFDR = 9.61× 10-6), CCBUM (OR 1.719, 95% CI 1.203-2.456; PFDR = 0.00679), and HCRIUM (OR 1.368, 95% CI 1.266-1.477; PFDR = 2.52 × 10-14) were used (Supplementary Data 1). Sensitivity analyses further confirmed the majority of these associations (Supplementary Data 1). Additionally, the MR‒Egger intercept test suggested potential horizontal pleiotropy for HCRIUM (PFDR for intercept < 0.05). Conversely, the IVW analysis demonstrated that gastric cancer might increase the risk of 13 cardiovascular-related factors, with the exception of vasodilators used in cardiac disease use measurement (VUCDUM). Detailed results from the five MR analysis methods are presented in Supplementary Data 1.

Cell type-specific enrichment of SNP heritability
In our analysis of 96 phenotypes, including gastric cancer, we further partitioned SNP heritability on the basis of six chromatin marks and nine cell types. We found that gastric cancer was enriched across all six chromatin marks, specifically in stomach tissues or cell types. The enrichment patterns of cardiovascular-related traits, such as blood pressure, were similar across all the chromatin markers, predominantly in the kidney, adrenal glands, heart, atria, and aorta. Additionally, we observed significant genetic enrichment for diabetes-related traits in gastrointestinal tissues (such as the small intestine, stomach, and colon) and the pancreas. Interestingly, angina pectoris and myocardial infarction displayed strong similarities only in the H3K9AC chromatin mark, with enrichment in cardiovascular-related tissues or cell types such as the right ventricle, right atrium, and left ventricle (Supplementary Fig. S1).

Multitrait analysis of gastric cancer and corresponding risk factors
Motivated by the findings from genetic correlation analyses, we conducted a comprehensive investigation into potential genetic factors shared between gastric cancer and its genetically correlated traits, aiming to identify novel susceptibility loci associated with gastric cancer risk. Guided by the 25 traits significantly correlated with gastric cancer (LDSC PFDR < 0.05), we performed a joint analysis using MTAG to identify SNPs that reached genome-wide significance (P < 5×10-8). Our analysis revealed 76 signals among gastric cancer and 25 traits in East Asians, including 41 previously reported loci, 26 novel findings, and 9 located within the MHC region (Supplementary Data 2). Notably, a novel locus at 12q22 (rs12814712) was identified in the MTAG analyses that linked gastric cancer with AP, MI, and SADUM (Fig. 3A-C). Considering that 25 phenotypes were analysed—albeit not fully independent—we additionally applied a Bonferroni-corrected threshold to account for multiple trait testing (P < 2×10⁻⁹). Under this stricter criterion, rs12814712 remained significantly associated with gastric cancer and MI. To further investigate this genomic region, we employed LocusZoom 13 to visualize the genetic associations, which highlighted a distinct signal surrounding the NDUFA12-VEZT locus across all four traits (Fig. 4A-D). We subsequently utilized LocusCompare 14 to assess the colocalization of these associated signals at 12q22, which demonstrated strong colocalization among gastric cancer, angina pectoris (AP), myocardial infarction (MI), and salicylic acid and derivatives use measurement (SADUM) (Fig. 5A-C). To further validate this association, we evaluated rs12814712 in an independent GWAS in a Korean cohort. A similar direction of effect was observed (BETA = 0.066), which was consistent with the results of the GC-BBJ analysis (BETA = 0.079; P = 7.65×10⁻⁵) (Supplementary Data 2). However, owing to the limited number of cases (n = 378), the association did not reach statistical significance. Interestingly, a nearby SNP, rs9634181, exhibited a stronger association (BETA = 0.19, P = 0.012) and was in weak linkage disequilibrium with rs12814712 (R² = 0.1; Supplementary Fig. S2A). Similarly, in the European-ancestry Million Veteran Program (MVP) cohort (n = 1,152), a nominally significant association was observed with a nearby SNP, rs183275771 (BETA = 0.081, P = 0.005), which was in linkage disequilibrium with rs12814712 (R² = 0.2; Supplementary Fig. S2B). These results suggested that increasing the sample size might yield statistically significant replication.

Additionally, we have summarized previously reported susceptibility loci for gastric cancer identified through GWAS in Table 1.

Expression Quantitative Trait Locus (eQTL) Analysis of the Gastric Cancer Risk SNP rs12814712 and Neighbouring Genes in the Chinese Population
We next analysed a cohort of 46 gastric cancer specimens using Sanger sequencing. This experimental validation was designed to assess whether the locus of interest could affect gene expression in gastric cancer. Among these samples, the AG variant of rs12814712 was found in 34.8% (16 cases), while the GG variant was observed in 65.2% (30 cases) (Fig. 6A). The detailed clinical characteristics of these 46 samples are described in Supplementary Table S2. The aforementioned signal at 12q22 (rs12814712) in gastric cancer covered four genes, namely, NDUFA12, FGD6, NR2C1, and VEZT. Multiple lines of evidence suggest that these genes may be involved in the pathogenesis of various cancers, including gastric cancer 15-20. To identify the genes potentially regulated by rs12814712 in gastric cancer, we used RT‒qPCR to compare the expression levels of four genes near rs12814712—NDUFA12, FGD6, NR2C1, and VEZT—in gastric cancer tissues and adjacent noncancerous tissues between the AG and GG groups. The expression levels of FGD6, VEZT, and NR2C1 were significantly lower in both adjacent nontumour tissues and gastric cancer tissues from patients with the AG genotype of rs12814712 than in those from patients with the GG genotype (P < 0.05; Fig. 6B and 6C). These findings suggested a potential relationship between the rs12814712 genotype and the regulation of these genes in both nontumour and tumour contexts.

Potential Regulatory Effect of rs12814712(G>A) on the Transcriptional Activity of Neighbouring Genes
To investigate whether rs12814712 had a cis-regulatory function, we first determined its genomic location. It was located in the 12q22 region, downstream of NDUFA12, NR2C1 and FGD6, and upstream of VEZT (Fig. 4). On the basis of its distribution between these genes, we designed two different luciferase reporter assay systems to evaluate the potential regulatory role of this region: (1) A 2001-bp genomic fragment containing the rs12814712 locus (wild-type WT‑G or mutant MUT‑A) and its flanking sequences (GRCh38/hg38 coordinates: chr12:94965934–94967934) was cloned upstream of the SV40 promoter to detect whether this fragment possesses enhancer-like activity (Supplementary Fig. S3A), and (2) the same fragment was inserted into the downstream end of the luciferase gene in the pmirGLO vector to examine its potential to regulate reporter gene expression in a downstream context (Supplementary Fig. S3B). Notably, this study aimed to functionally validate the region containing rs12814712 as an independent noncoding fragment to explore whether it could exert cis-regulatory effects at the transcriptional level. In the enhancer reporter system, the MUT (A) allele significantly reduced luciferase activity (P < 0.05), suggesting that this fragment possessed enhancer-like activity and that the A allele impaired this function (Supplementary Fig. S3C). In contrast, no significant difference was observed between the two alleles (WT and MUT) in the pmirGLO system, which indicated that the fragment did not exhibit significant posttranscriptional regulatory effects under these conditions (Supplementary Fig. S3D). Given that our GWAS signal was located upstream of VEZT and downstream of NR2C1, FGD6, and NDUFA12, this finding supported our eQTL results, indicating a regulatory relationship between the rs12814712 A allele and the expression of VEZT. Taken together, these results suggested that the genomic region containing rs12814712 might play a role in cis-regulation with enhancer-like activity.

Association of genes near rs12814712 with proliferation and migration capacity in gastric cancer
To investigate the role of potential target genes near rs12814712 in gastric cancer, we conducted a series of in vitro experiments using AGS and MKN45 gastric cancer cell lines. NDUFA12, FGD6, NR2C1, and VEZT overexpression models were established via plasmid transfection, with successful overexpression confirmed by RT–qPCR (Fig. 7A). Cell viability assays indicated that overexpression of NR2C1 and VEZT significantly reduced cell proliferation, while NDUFA12 and FGD6 had no notable effect (Fig. 7B). This antiproliferative effect was further supported by the results of EdU assays, which revealed a significant reduction in the percentage of proliferating NR2C1- and VEZT-overexpressing cells but not in that of NDUFA12- and FGD6-overexpressing cells (Fig. 7C). Consistently, the results of the colony formation assays revealed that NR2C1 and VEZT markedly inhibited the colony-forming ability of both cell lines (Fig. 7D). Migration assays, including wound healing and Transwell assays, demonstrated that overexpression of NR2C1 and VEZT significantly impaired cell migration, whereas NDUFA12 and FGD6 did not affect migratory capacity (Fig. 8A and B).

To further validate the tumour-suppressive roles of VEZT and NR2C1, we performed gene knockdown experiments using two independent short hairpin RNAs (shRNAs) targeting each gene (Supplementary Fig. S4A). Silencing of either VEZT or NR2C1 significantly increased gastric cancer cell proliferation, as demonstrated by cell growth and colony formation assays (Supplementary Fig. S4B–D), and enhanced cell migration capacity (Supplementary Fig. S5A–B), which was consistent with the results observed in the overexpression experiments.
paper_content.methods:
Ethical compliance
All research involving human participants complied with all relevant ethical regulations. The study protocol (YXLL-KY-2022(068)) was approved by the Institutional Review Board of the First Affiliated Hospital of Shandong First Medical University (Jinan, China). Written informed consent was obtained from all participants, and the study was conducted in accordance with the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki.

GWAS data
The GWAS data for gastric cancer in East Asian populations included 167,122 individuals, including 7,921 cases and 159,201 controls. Additionally, we obtained summary statistics for 95 phenotypes (including diseases, biomarkers, and medication usage) with case numbers greater than 3,000 from the 220 phenotypes available in the BBJ database 36. In BBJ, genotyping was conducted using Illumina arrays, and genotype imputation was performed using the 1000 Genomes Phase 3 reference panel combined with Japanese whole-genome sequencing data. Variants with an imputation of Rsq ≥ 0.7 were retained. Phenotypes were derived from curated medical records, ATC-coded medication data, and biomarker measurements, with appropriate outlier removal and medication-specific adjustments. A GWAS for binary traits employed SAIGE to account for sample relatedness and case‒control imbalance, whereas BOLT-LMM was used for quantitative traits with adjustments for age, sex, and principal components. A comprehensive overview of the included GWAS datasets from East Asian populations is provided in Supplementary Data 3. To validate our findings, we utilized two independent cohorts: the Korean Genome and Epidemiology Study (KoGES) cohort, comprising 378 gastric cancer cases and 71,920 controls of East Asian ancestry, and the Million Veteran Program (MVP) cohort, comprising 1,152 cases and 449,540 controls of predominantly European ancestry.

Global genetic correlation analysis
Genetic correlation (rg) between each pair of diseases or traits was assessed using LD score regression (LDSC) with GWAS summary statistics 37. The equation used in the LDSC was as follows: 𝑬[𝜷𝒋𝜸𝒋] = 𝑵𝒔𝒓𝒈𝒍𝒋 / 𝑴 + 𝑵𝟏𝑵𝟐𝒓𝒈𝒍𝒋 / 𝑴 √𝑵𝟏𝑵𝟐, where 𝛽𝑗 and 𝛾𝑗 represent the effect sizes of SNP j on the two traits being tested, 𝑁1 and 𝑁2 are the sample sizes for the two traits, 𝑁𝑠 is the number of overlapping samples between the two traits, r is the phenotypic correlation in the overlapping samples, and 𝑙𝑗 is the LD score. In line with the authors’ recommendations, we used the default LDSC regression weights and limited the analysis to SNPs with an MAF > 5% in the reference panel for estimation.

In this analysis, precalculated linkage disequilibrium scores for HapMap3 SNPs were utilized. These scores were derived from individuals of Asian ancestry from the 1000 Genomes Project. SNP markers with an imputation INFO score less than 0.9 were excluded from the analysis. LDSC was also employed to estimate the SNP-based heritability of the examined traits 37.

Cell type-specific enrichment of SNP heritability
Stratified LDSC (S-LDSC) was employed in this study to identify specific functional categories or cell types that significantly affect the heritability of the traits under investigation. The baseline v1.1 model, which contains 53 functional annotations, including gene regions, conserved elements, and regulatory features, was used as the reference in all S-LDSC analyses to account for known sources of heritability 38. The annotation data used in this analysis were obtained from the Roadmap project and included information on six chromatin marks (DHS, H3K27ac, H3K36me3, H3K4me1, H3K4me3, and H3K9ac) across a diverse set of 88 cell types or tissues. These annotations were subsequently used to partition the SNP heritability of each trait. Additionally, the cell type annotations were grouped into nine categories, namely, adipose, central nervous system (CNS), digestive system, cardiovascular, musculoskeletal and connective tissue, immune and blood, liver, pancreas, and others. We visualized the annotation-specific enrichment values using a colour-scaled heatmap generated by the ComplexHeatmap package (v2.12.1) in R 4.2.3. The hierarchical clustering of annotations was performed on the basis of Euclidean distance metrics with complete linkage agglomeration, implementing the default clustering algorithm (hclust) within the ComplexHeatmap framework.

Multitrait analysis of GWAS (MTAG)
MTAG was employed to explore the genetic associations between gastric cancer and each of the other phenotypes separately by leveraging combined GWAS summary statistics from gastric cancer and one additional trait in each analysis 10. This approach enhances the ability to detect genetic loci associated with correlated traits by addressing sample overlap and incomplete genetic correlation. For the MTAG analysis, we used default parameters, including a genetic correlation prior of N (0,1), and applied cross-trait LD score regression intercepts to account for residual sample overlap. In the initial step of MTAG, variants were filtered by excluding noncommon SNPs, duplicated SNPs, or those with strand ambiguity. The pairwise genetic correlation between traits was subsequently estimated using LDSC, and these estimates were then used to calibrate the variance‒covariance matrix of the random effect component. Following calibration, a random-effects meta-analysis was performed by MTAG to generate SNP-level summary statistics. The suggestive significance threshold (P < 0.01) in single-trait GWAS was selected to capture potentially meaningful associations while maintaining stringency, as these signals were further validated by genome-wide significance in multitrait analysis. Pleiotropic SNPs that achieved genome-wide significance (P< 5×10–8) in the multitrait analysis and suggestive significance (P< 0.01) in the single-trait GWAS were prioritized. The major histocompatibility complex (MHC) region was treated as one locus because of its complex LD structure.

Two-sample Mendelian Randomization
In the two-sample Mendelian randomization (MR) analysis, we implemented five widely recognized statistical methods: inverse-variance weighted (IVW), MR‒Egger, weighted median, simple mode, and weighted mode. The IVW method, which served as the primary analytical approach, was applied under a multiplicative random effects model to estimate the causal association between genetic predisposition to gastric cancer and cardiovascular-related risk factors identified through the LDSC. The IVW method assumes no intercept term and employs the inverse of the variance as weights to optimize model fitting. To address potential pleiotropic effects, sensitivity analyses were conducted using the MR‒Egger method 39, which incorporates a weighted linear regression framework to detect and adjust for horizontal pleiotropy among the instrumental variables (IVs). The results are reported as odds ratios (ORs) with corresponding 95% confidence intervals (CIs), and statistical significance was defined as P < 0.05. All MR analyses were executed using the TwoSampleMR package in R software (version 4.0.2), ensuring robust and reproducible causal inference 40.

Patients and tissue samples
Human tissue samples for this study were obtained from a prospective cohort of 46 patients who underwent radical gastrectomy at the First Affiliated Hospital of Shandong First Medical University (Jinan, China) in 2023. For each patient, paired samples of primary gastric cancer tissue and matched adjacent non-tumourous gastric mucosa were collected. The cohort included 33 male and 13 female patients. The genotypic distribution of the rs12814712 variant was as follows: AG genotype (9 males, 7 females) and GG genotype (24 males, 6 females). The participant age distribution is provided in Supplementary Table S2. Sex was determined according to hospital medical records. Although sex was not incorporated as a biological variable in the primary genetic association study design, all clinical data were sex-disaggregated in the source material.

Written informed consent was obtained from all participants for the use of their tissue samples and associated clinical data for research purposes. No financial compensation was provided. Following collection, genomic DNA and total RNA were extracted from portions of the tissue samples for downstream analyses. The original tissue samples were not completely consumed during this process. Residual tissue materials (aliquots and tissue blocks) were cryopreserved and permanently stored at –80 °C in the institutional biobank of the First Affiliated Hospital of Shandong First Medical University.

These deidentified biospecimens and associated clinical data remain available for academic validation and collaborative research. Access requests can be submitted with a scientifically justified proposal and completion of a material transfer agreement (MTA). All such requests should be directed to the corresponding author, Guangyong Zhang (guangyongzhang@hotmail.com), for review and facilitation.

PCR-Sanger sequencing of rs12814712
We collected 25 mg of cancer tissue from each of the 46 gastric cancer patients and extracted genomic DNA using the Ezup Column Animal Genomic DNA Purification Kit (B518251; Sangon Biotech, China). The extracted genomic DNA was amplified by PCR, and the PCR amplification primers for the rs12814712 locus were as follows: forward primer (5’ to 3’): TCATACTATGGGCAACTTGGCAC; reverse primer (5’ to 3’): CGGCAGCCCAGAACAGTAAA. The PCR reaction mix included the following components: 10x Taq buffer (with MgCl2), 10 µM dNTPs (mix), forward and reverse primers at 10 μM, 1 μl of template genomic DNA, 5 U/μl Taq DNA polymerase, and sterile water added to a final volume of 25 µL. After amplification, the PCR products were purified by agarose gel electrophoresis, and the sequence of the PCR amplification products was detected by Sanger sequencing.

Quantitative Real-Time PCR
Total RNA was extracted from frozen gastric cancer tissue or cell lines with TRIzol reagent (G3013; Servicebio, Wuhan, China). Single-strand complementary DNA (cDNA) was synthesized with a ReverTra Ace qPCR RT Kit (FSQ-101; TOYOBO Co., Ltd., Osaka, Japan). For quantitative real-time PCR, SYBR Green Real-time PCR Master Mix (QPK-201; TOYOBO Co., Ltd.) was used following the manufacturer’s instructions. The total PCR volume was 20 μl, containing 0.1 μl of each primer. The target-specific primers used were designed by Huada Gene (Shenzhen, China), and the specific sequences are listed in Supplementary Table S3.

Cell culture
The HEK293T, AGS, and MKN45 cell lines were obtained from Procell (Wuhan, China) and cultured in DMEM (for HEK293T), Ham's F-12K (for AGS), or RPMI-1640 (for MKN45) medium (all from Gibco, Carlsbad, CA, USA), each supplemented with 10% foetal bovine serum (FBS; Gibco) and 1% penicillin/streptomycin (Gibco). The cells were incubated at 37°C in 5% CO₂. The identity of all the cell lines was verified by short tandem repeat (STR) analysis, and the cell lines were routinely screened for mycoplasma contamination.

Plasmid Constructs
For luciferase assay-related plasmids, the 2001-bp genomic fragment containing the rs12814712 (G>A) site and 1000-bp flanking sequences was cloned and inserted into 1) the pGL3-promoter vector (E1761; Promega, Madison, WI, USA) to assess its potential enhancer-like activity and 2) the pmirGLO vector (E1330; Promega, Madison, WI, USA) to simulate its regulatory ability in a downstream context (fragment sequences are shown in Supplementary Data 4). The SV40 promoter sequence was used in these two plasmids to determine promoter function (Supplementary Fig. S3A-B).

For gene loss- and gain-of-function assays, plasmids were constructed by LST Biotech (Shandong Co., Ltd., Jinan, China). For gene knockdown experiments, short hairpin RNA (shRNA) sequences targeting NR2C1 and VEZT (Supplementary Table S4) were cloned and inserted into the pLKO.1-EGFP vector. For gene overexpression, the full-length coding sequences of NDUFA12, FGD6, NR2C1, and VEZT were cloned and inserted into the corresponding expression vectors. Information on the sequences and vectors is provided in Supplementary Table S5. The newly constructed plasmids generated in this study are available from the corresponding author upon reasonable request for academic research.

Luciferase Assays
HEK293T and AGS cells (1×10⁵/well) were taken in 96-well plates and were transfected after 18 h of incubation, pGL3 constructs were transfected with 0.1 μg test plasmid plus 0.01 μg pRL-TK plasmid, and pmirGLO constructs were transfected with test plasmid alone. Luciferase activity was measured using a Dual-Luciferase® Reporter Assay System kit (E1910; Promega, Madison, WI, USA): cells were lysed with 20 μL of PLB (15 min of RT shaking), after which firefly (luciferase assay reagent II) and Renilla (Stop & Glo) luminescence was sequentially measured. Relative activity was calculated as the Firefly/Renilla ratio. The experiments were repeated in triplicate.

Cell transfection
Cells were seeded in 6-well plates (5 × 105 cells/well) and incubated for 18 h. Then, overexpression plasmids for the indicated genes (NDUFA12, FGD6, NR2C1, and VEZT) and knockdown plasmids for the indicated genes (NR2C1 and VEZT) were transfected using Lipofectamine 2000 (11668030; Invitrogen, Carlsbad, CA, USA) and Opti-MEM™ I (31985062; Invitrogen, Carlsbad, CA, USA) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. After the cells were incubated for 8 h, the medium was replaced with Ham's F-12K (for AGS) or 1640 medium (for MKN45) supplemented with 10% FBS. The sequences of the shRNAs for NR2C1 and VEZT are listed in Supplementary Table S4.

Cellular viability assay
Approximately 24 hours after transfection, 5000 cells were seeded into 96-well plates. Cell viability was then evaluated at 0, 24, and 48 hours using the Cell Counting Kit-8 (CCK-8) assay (CK04, Dojindo Laboratories, Kumamoto, Japan), following the methods described previously 41. After a 2-hour incubation, cellular viability was assessed using a microplate reader, and the absorbance was measured at a wavelength of 450 nm.

EdU staining
In accordance with the manufacturer's instructions, cell proliferation was assessed using an EdU staining kit (C0071S; Beyotime, Shanghai, China). Cells (1 × 104) in each group were incubated with EdU buffer (10 μM) at 37°C for 2 hours. The supernatant was then discarded, and the cells were washed twice with PBS, followed by fixation with paraformaldehyde for 20 min. Afterwards, the mixture was incubated with freshly prepared cocktail buffer. To calculate the proportion of EdU-positive cells, the number of fluorescently stained cells was divided by the number of DAPI-stained cells. The nuclei were then stained with DAPI (C1006; Beyotime, Shanghai, China). The cells were observed and photographed under a fluorescence microscope. EdU was excited by light at a wavelength of 488 nm to emit green fluorescence, while DAPI was excited by light at a wavelength of 340 nm to emit blue fluorescence.

Colony formation assay
Twenty-four hours after transfection, the transfected gastric cancer cells (1 × 103) were seeded into 6-well plates. After an additional 14 days of culture, the cells were fixed and stained with 1% crystal violet (Solarbio, Beijing, China). After being stained with crystal violet for 20 min, the colonies formed were counted.

Transwell assay
Transwell assays were conducted to evaluate the migration and invasion of AGS and MKN45 cells. For the migration assay, cells (4 × 104) were suspended in serum-free medium (120 μL) and added to the upper chamber. Medium containing 10% FBS (750 μL) was added to the lower chamber to induce cell migration. The cells that migrated were washed three times with PBS, fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde for 30 minutes, and stained with 1% crystal violet. Images were observed at 100× magnification.

Wound healing assay
Cells (6 × 105) were cultured on 6-well plates. A pipette tip was subsequently used to scratch the bottom of the plate. Free cells were washed away with PBS buffer. The migration distance was observed at 0 h and 48 h.

Statistics & Reproducibility
The overall study design involved computational analysis of population-level genetic data (GWAS) followed by experimental validation in independent patient tissues and cell line models. No statistical method was used to predetermine sample size for the GWAS analyses, as these utilized all available data from the specified biobanks (BBJ, KoGES, MVP). The sample size for the patient tissue cohort (n=46) was based on availability during the study period. No data were excluded from the GWAS summary statistics analyses. For cellular and molecular experiments, sample sizes were determined on the basis of common practices in the field to ensure adequate power for detecting effects, and all experiments were performed with at least three biological replicates. The experiments were not randomized. The investigators were not blinded to allocation during the experiments or outcome assessment. Statistical analyses were conducted using SPSS software (version 22.0) and GraphPad Prism (version 8.0). Data from cellular and molecular experiments are presented as the mean ± standard deviation (SD). Group differences were evaluated using one-way ANOVA. Significance levels in the figures are denoted as follows: *P < 0.05, **P < 0.01, and ***P < 0.001. To control for multiple comparisons in the genome-wide analyses (genetic correlation via LDSC, S-LDSC, and Mendelian randomization), Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) correction was applied, with significance defined as PFDR < 0.05.

Data availability
The GWAS summary statistics data used in this study are available in the GWAS Catalogue under the accession codes summarized in Supplementary Data 3 [https://www.ebi.ac.uk/gwas/]. The individual-level genotype and gene expression data generated in this study are available under restricted access to protect patient privacy and comply with ethical regulations; access can be obtained by submitting a formal request to the corresponding author, Dr. Guangyong Zhang (guangyongzhang@hotmail.com), for academic, noncommercial research purposes, which will then be reviewed by the Ethics Committee of The First Affiliated Hospital of Shandong First Medical University. A completed data transfer agreement may be needed. The raw individual-level clinical data are protected and are not available because of data privacy laws. Source data are provided with this paper.

Code availability
We conducted our analyses using a variety of publicly available software tools. The computational environment consisted of Python (v2.7.18), Perl (v5.16.3), and R (v4.2.3). Genetic correlation analyses between gastric cancer and 95 traits were conducted using LDSC v1.0.1, with subsequent S-LDSC to evaluate cell type-specific SNP heritability enrichment. Bidirectional Mendelian randomization was implemented through the TwoSampleMR R package (v0.6.4). For the multitrait GWAS meta-analysis of gastric cancer and its 25 genetically correlated traits, we employed MTAG v1.0.8. The custom scripts used in this study are deposited in Zenodo and are publicly accessible at https://zenodo.org/records/18085131.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
This is an interesting study, adding to understanding of gastric cancer risk through GWAS, multi-trait analyses and some
functional work. I have some questions to clarify analysis reporting and some concerns for the functional analysis.
The Mendelian randomization analyses consistently state that cardiovascular traits are associated with increased gastric
cancer risk. However, this is at odds with the ORs provided, that are all below 1, indicating reduced risk. Can the authors
please clarify the direction of effect presented? If the ORs are correct, they would also not align with the positive correlation
observed using LDSR.
Although promising, MTAG results should be interpreted with caution due to high chance of false positive reporting – where
loci are associated due to the strong influence of other included factors, rather than the focal trait. The authors should make
this clear in the limitation of the manuscript. Usually there would be an attempt to replicate findings in another dataset. There
are several publicly available GWAS datasets for gastric cancer, have the authors accessed any to evaluate whether this
loci displays any evidence of an association with gastric cancer, or whether it is in the same direction? The allele frequency
for rs12814712 looks pretty stable across all ethnicities so I strongly encourage the authors to do this.
The negative genetic correlation observed between gastric cancer and lung and colorectal cancer seems surprising, and
deserves to be highlighted in the discussion. Although gastric cancer wasn’t included, a large multi-cancer analysis (12 solid
tumors) that performed pairwise genetic correlations found largely all cancers were positively correlated, albeit not all
significantly (Lindstrom et al JNCI 2023).
The eQTL analysis and other analyses performed using the tissue cohort is very weak, comprising only 46 samples. The
authors don’t appear to adequately acknowledge the sample size limitation. It is difficult to draw meaningful results from
these data. Again, given the stable allele frequency across ethnicities, the authors should attempt validation using another
cohort, such as TCGA.
Due to the above, the evidence linking the variant to these genes is rather weak, would suggest that a luciferase promoter
reporter gene assay would be a better method to provide evidence for SNP functionality.
The samples don’t appear to be matched but collected prospectively. Indeed, there is a significant difference in those that
had lymph node metastasis. Was there any adjustment for this in the differential expression analysis? It is a strong call to
suggest that >140 genes were significantly differentially expressed due to a risk variant which would normally have a small
effect on risk? It would appear more likely to me that the DE genes are more likely representing lymph node metastasis, in
general and perhaps nothing to do with the SNP. On a different note, were your potential target genes at your locus
differentially expressed?

number of samples collected.
Lines 299-301: the authors mention requiring validation in East Asians due to varying LD patterns, however they haven’t
provided any comparison of the LD pattern across populations in at this locus.
The direction of effect for the risk variant and gene effects requires clarification. The authors observed the gastric cancer risk
allele associates with increased expression of their target genes, however expression of two of these genes (VEZT and
NR2C1) displayed anti-cancer effects (inhibition of proliferation and migration). This is not consistent with the eQTL effect.

Are results throughout manuscript adjusted for multiple testing (e.g. MR analysis, gene correlations, stratified LDSC)?
What was the criteria used for a trait to be included in the MTAG analysis? E.g. rg threshold, p-value)

Additionally, we used the pmirGLO vector (Cat. E1330, Promega,
Madison, WI, USA), which also contains an SV40 promoter and the

You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Gastric cancer is a leading cause of cancer-related death, particularly in East Asia, yet its genetic basis remains incompletely understood. Using genome-wide association study data from BioBank Japan, we show that gastric cancer shares significant genetic associations with 25 other phenotypes, most notably cardiovascular conditions such as angina pectoris and myocardial infarction. Mendelian randomization supports a causal role of these traits in gastric cancer risk. Multitrait analysis of GWAS reveals a novel pleiotropic locus at 12q22 (rs12814712) that is shared between gastric cancer and cardiovascular traits. Functional experiments demonstrate that the risk allele at this locus reduces transcriptional activity and downregulates the expression of nearby genes, particularly VEZT. In gastric cancer cells, overexpression of VEZT and NR2C1 suppress proliferation and migration, whereas their knockdown promotes malignancy. Our analysis identifies rs12814712 as a novel susceptibility locus for gastric cancer and underscores its regulatory role in disease-related gene networks.

---

## Introduction

According to global cancer statistics for 2022, gastric cancer ranks fifth in terms of both incidence and mortality worldwide, accounting for 968,350 new cases and 659,853 deaths, respectively 1. The incidence of gastric cancer varies regionally, with higher rates in East Asia and Eastern Europe and lower rates in Northern Europe and North America 1, which are likely influenced by environmental, lifestyle, and genetic factors. Empirical studies have shown that gastric cancer is the result of a complex interaction of genetic and environmental risk factors 2. Risk factors encompass a spectrum ranging from Helicobacter pylori (HP) infection to dietary habits such as the consumption of pickled foods, as well as behaviours such as alcohol consumption and tobacco use. Among these, HP infection emerges as the most influential determinant. Moreover, genetic studies, including twin and genome-wide association studies (GWASs), have revealed a substantial genetic contribution to gastric cancer susceptibility, with heritability estimates of approximately 20.9% in the Chinese population and 22% in Nordic twins 3,4.

Gastric cancer displays substantial polygenicity, with East Asian populations showing the identification of at least 15 risk loci through GWAS. For instance, in a two-stage GWAS in Japan, a notable association was found between an intronic SNP (rs2976392) within the PSCA gene and diffuse-type gastric cancer 5. Similarly, researchers at Nanjing Medical University reported genetic variations at loci 1p35.2 and 6p22.1 in the Chinese population, which correlated with increased gastric cancer risk 6. Moreover, they elucidated the roles of PRKAA1 at the 5p13.1 locus and NOC3L at the 10q23.33 locus in gastric tumour pathogenesis 7. In contrast, only the 11q22.3 locus was identified in Europeans 8. Furthermore, several genes within these risk loci, such as MUC1 (1q22), SPOCD1 (1p35.2), PSCA (8q24.3), PRKAA1 (5p13.1), BTN3A2 (6p22.1), and NOC3L (10q23.33), have been functionally validated as susceptibility genes for gastric cancer 5-7,9.

Recent advances in statistical methodologies for GWAS analyses have made it possible to conduct joint analyses of traits that share genetic architecture 10. Through meta-analyses of GWAS summary statistics for genetically correlated traits, multitrait analysis of GWAS (MTAG) not only enhances statistical power but also identifies pleiotropic genetic variants that influence interconnected traits. This cross-trait analysis approach has proven successful in numerous cancer research studies. Additionally, it has been applied to the investigation of seven upper gastrointestinal disorders 11. However, to the best of our knowledge, no multitrait GWAS analysis specifically targeting gastric cancer has been conducted to date.

In this study, we identified multiple novel pleiotropic loci associated with gastric cancer using GWAS data from the BioBank Japan (BBJ) 12. Notably, we observed that several genes adjacent to these loci might be involved in gastric cancer pathogenesis, as documented in the literature. We collected gastric cancer samples and conducted functional experiments to elucidate the regulatory relationships between the identified loci and their neighbouring genes, as well as to explore the potential roles of candidate genes in the aetiology of gastric cancer.

---

## Results

In this study, we utilized GWAS data from BBJ and identified multiple new pleiotropic loci associated with gastric cancer using MTAG. Notably, we observed that several genes near the novel 12q22 locus might be involved in the pathogenesis of gastric cancer. Consequently, we collected clinical gastric cancer samples and conducted functional experiments to elucidate the potential regulatory relationships between the identified loci and their neighbouring genes and to explore the potential roles of candidate genes in the aetiology of gastric cancer. An overview of our study is provided in Fig. 1.

Genetic correlations between gastric cancer and associated phenotypes
We analysed GWAS data from BBJ to explore the genetic correlation between gastric cancer and 95 phenotypes, including diseases, biomarkers, and medication usage, in East Asians. Following multiple testing correction, our analysis revealed a significant positive genetic correlation between gastric cancer and 25 cardiovascular-related traits, including diseases like angina pectoris (AP, rg = 0.4611, PFDR = 0.0001), myocardial infarction (MI, rg = 0.3415, PFDR = 0.0009), blood pressure measurements such as diastolic blood pressure (DBP, rg = 0.2549, PFDR = 0.0028), systolic blood pressure (SBP, rg = 0.2421, PFDR = 0.001), and mean arterial pressure (MAP, rg = 0.2612, PFDR = 0.0009), as well as the use of cardiovascular drugs like calcium channel blockers (CCBUM, rg = 0.3561, PFDR = 4.56 × 10-7), renin-angiotensin system inhibitors (AARSUM, rg = 0.4309, PFDR = 1.41 × 10-8), HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors (HCRIUM, rg = 0.3786, PFDR = 1.82 × 10-6) and salicylic acid and derivatives (SADUM, rg = 0.4115, PFDR = 0.0002). Additionally, positive genetic correlations were identified between gastric cancer and other cancer types, including lung cancer (LC, rg = 0.7442, PFDR = 0.0058) and colorectal cancer (CRC, rg = 0.3043, PFDR = 0.002) (Supplementary Table S1, Fig. 2).

Causal Impact of Cardiovascular-Related Factors on Gastric Cancer
To further investigate the relationship between cardiovascular traits and gastric cancer, we conducted Mendelian randomization (MR) analysis. The inverse-variance weighted (IVW) method revealed that after false discovery rate (FDR) correction, eight cardiovascular-related factors were significantly associated with an increased risk of gastric cancer, including AP (OR 1.289, 95% CI 1.060–1.568; PFDR = 0.0192), stable angina pectoris (SAP, OR 1.408, 95% CI 1.243–1.596; PFDR = 5.56 × 10-7), and MI (OR 1.179, 95% CI 1.094–1.270; PFDR = 5.36 × 10-5). Additionally, antithrombotic agents (AAUM, OR 1.829; 95% CI 1.343-2.493; PFDR = 3.61 × 10-4), beta-blocking agents (BBAUM, OR 1.478, 95% CI 1.108-1.972; PFDR = 0.0159), SADUM (OR 1.799, 95% CI 1.412-2.293; PFDR = 9.61× 10-6), CCBUM (OR 1.719, 95% CI 1.203-2.456; PFDR = 0.00679), and HCRIUM (OR 1.368, 95% CI 1.266-1.477; PFDR = 2.52 × 10-14) were used (Supplementary Data 1). Sensitivity analyses further confirmed the majority of these associations (Supplementary Data 1). Additionally, the MR‒Egger intercept test suggested potential horizontal pleiotropy for HCRIUM (PFDR for intercept < 0.05). Conversely, the IVW analysis demonstrated that gastric cancer might increase the risk of 13 cardiovascular-related factors, with the exception of vasodilators used in cardiac disease use measurement (VUCDUM). Detailed results from the five MR analysis methods are presented in Supplementary Data 1.

Cell type-specific enrichment of SNP heritability
In our analysis of 96 phenotypes, including gastric cancer, we further partitioned SNP heritability on the basis of six chromatin marks and nine cell types. We found that gastric cancer was enriched across all six chromatin marks, specifically in stomach tissues or cell types. The enrichment patterns of cardiovascular-related traits, such as blood pressure, were similar across all the chromatin markers, predominantly in the kidney, adrenal glands, heart, atria, and aorta. Additionally, we observed significant genetic enrichment for diabetes-related traits in gastrointestinal tissues (such as the small intestine, stomach, and colon) and the pancreas. Interestingly, angina pectoris and myocardial infarction displayed strong similarities only in the H3K9AC chromatin mark, with enrichment in cardiovascular-related tissues or cell types such as the right ventricle, right atrium, and left ventricle (Supplementary Fig. S1).

Multitrait analysis of gastric cancer and corresponding risk factors
Motivated by the findings from genetic correlation analyses, we conducted a comprehensive investigation into potential genetic factors shared between gastric cancer and its genetically correlated traits, aiming to identify novel susceptibility loci associated with gastric cancer risk. Guided by the 25 traits significantly correlated with gastric cancer (LDSC PFDR < 0.05), we performed a joint analysis using MTAG to identify SNPs that reached genome-wide significance (P < 5×10-8). Our analysis revealed 76 signals among gastric cancer and 25 traits in East Asians, including 41 previously reported loci, 26 novel findings, and 9 located within the MHC region (Supplementary Data 2). Notably, a novel locus at 12q22 (rs12814712) was identified in the MTAG analyses that linked gastric cancer with AP, MI, and SADUM (Fig. 3A-C). Considering that 25 phenotypes were analysed—albeit not fully independent—we additionally applied a Bonferroni-corrected threshold to account for multiple trait testing (P < 2×10⁻⁹). Under this stricter criterion, rs12814712 remained significantly associated with gastric cancer and MI. To further investigate this genomic region, we employed LocusZoom 13 to visualize the genetic associations, which highlighted a distinct signal surrounding the NDUFA12-VEZT locus across all four traits (Fig. 4A-D). We subsequently utilized LocusCompare 14 to assess the colocalization of these associated signals at 12q22, which demonstrated strong colocalization among gastric cancer, angina pectoris (AP), myocardial infarction (MI), and salicylic acid and derivatives use measurement (SADUM) (Fig. 5A-C). To further validate this association, we evaluated rs12814712 in an independent GWAS in a Korean cohort. A similar direction of effect was observed (BETA = 0.066), which was consistent with the results of the GC-BBJ analysis (BETA = 0.079; P = 7.65×10⁻⁵) (Supplementary Data 2). However, owing to the limited number of cases (n = 378), the association did not reach statistical significance. Interestingly, a nearby SNP, rs9634181, exhibited a stronger association (BETA = 0.19, P = 0.012) and was in weak linkage disequilibrium with rs12814712 (R² = 0.1; Supplementary Fig. S2A). Similarly, in the European-ancestry Million Veteran Program (MVP) cohort (n = 1,152), a nominally significant association was observed with a nearby SNP, rs183275771 (BETA = 0.081, P = 0.005), which was in linkage disequilibrium with rs12814712 (R² = 0.2; Supplementary Fig. S2B). These results suggested that increasing the sample size might yield statistically significant replication.

Additionally, we have summarized previously reported susceptibility loci for gastric cancer identified through GWAS in Table 1.

Expression Quantitative Trait Locus (eQTL) Analysis of the Gastric Cancer Risk SNP rs12814712 and Neighbouring Genes in the Chinese Population
We next analysed a cohort of 46 gastric cancer specimens using Sanger sequencing. This experimental validation was designed to assess whether the locus of interest could affect gene expression in gastric cancer. Among these samples, the AG variant of rs12814712 was found in 34.8% (16 cases), while the GG variant was observed in 65.2% (30 cases) (Fig. 6A). The detailed clinical characteristics of these 46 samples are described in Supplementary Table S2. The aforementioned signal at 12q22 (rs12814712) in gastric cancer covered four genes, namely, NDUFA12, FGD6, NR2C1, and VEZT. Multiple lines of evidence suggest that these genes may be involved in the pathogenesis of various cancers, including gastric cancer 15-20. To identify the genes potentially regulated by rs12814712 in gastric cancer, we used RT‒qPCR to compare the expression levels of four genes near rs12814712—NDUFA12, FGD6, NR2C1, and VEZT—in gastric cancer tissues and adjacent noncancerous tissues between the AG and GG groups. The expression levels of FGD6, VEZT, and NR2C1 were significantly lower in both adjacent nontumour tissues and gastric cancer tissues from patients with the AG genotype of rs12814712 than in those from patients with the GG genotype (P < 0.05; Fig. 6B and 6C). These findings suggested a potential relationship between the rs12814712 genotype and the regulation of these genes in both nontumour and tumour contexts.

Potential Regulatory Effect of rs12814712(G>A) on the Transcriptional Activity of Neighbouring Genes
To investigate whether rs12814712 had a cis-regulatory function, we first determined its genomic location. It was located in the 12q22 region, downstream of NDUFA12, NR2C1 and FGD6, and upstream of VEZT (Fig. 4). On the basis of its distribution between these genes, we designed two different luciferase reporter assay systems to evaluate the potential regulatory role of this region: (1) A 2001-bp genomic fragment containing the rs12814712 locus (wild-type WT‑G or mutant MUT‑A) and its flanking sequences (GRCh38/hg38 coordinates: chr12:94965934–94967934) was cloned upstream of the SV40 promoter to detect whether this fragment possesses enhancer-like activity (Supplementary Fig. S3A), and (2) the same fragment was inserted into the downstream end of the luciferase gene in the pmirGLO vector to examine its potential to regulate reporter gene expression in a downstream context (Supplementary Fig. S3B). Notably, this study aimed to functionally validate the region containing rs12814712 as an independent noncoding fragment to explore whether it could exert cis-regulatory effects at the transcriptional level. In the enhancer reporter system, the MUT (A) allele significantly reduced luciferase activity (P < 0.05), suggesting that this fragment possessed enhancer-like activity and that the A allele impaired this function (Supplementary Fig. S3C). In contrast, no significant difference was observed between the two alleles (WT and MUT) in the pmirGLO system, which indicated that the fragment did not exhibit significant posttranscriptional regulatory effects under these conditions (Supplementary Fig. S3D). Given that our GWAS signal was located upstream of VEZT and downstream of NR2C1, FGD6, and NDUFA12, this finding supported our eQTL results, indicating a regulatory relationship between the rs12814712 A allele and the expression of VEZT. Taken together, these results suggested that the genomic region containing rs12814712 might play a role in cis-regulation with enhancer-like activity.

Association of genes near rs12814712 with proliferation and migration capacity in gastric cancer
To investigate the role of potential target genes near rs12814712 in gastric cancer, we conducted a series of in vitro experiments using AGS and MKN45 gastric cancer cell lines. NDUFA12, FGD6, NR2C1, and VEZT overexpression models were established via plasmid transfection, with successful overexpression confirmed by RT–qPCR (Fig. 7A). Cell viability assays indicated that overexpression of NR2C1 and VEZT significantly reduced cell proliferation, while NDUFA12 and FGD6 had no notable effect (Fig. 7B). This antiproliferative effect was further supported by the results of EdU assays, which revealed a significant reduction in the percentage of proliferating NR2C1- and VEZT-overexpressing cells but not in that of NDUFA12- and FGD6-overexpressing cells (Fig. 7C). Consistently, the results of the colony formation assays revealed that NR2C1 and VEZT markedly inhibited the colony-forming ability of both cell lines (Fig. 7D). Migration assays, including wound healing and Transwell assays, demonstrated that overexpression of NR2C1 and VEZT significantly impaired cell migration, whereas NDUFA12 and FGD6 did not affect migratory capacity (Fig. 8A and B).

To further validate the tumour-suppressive roles of VEZT and NR2C1, we performed gene knockdown experiments using two independent short hairpin RNAs (shRNAs) targeting each gene (Supplementary Fig. S4A). Silencing of either VEZT or NR2C1 significantly increased gastric cancer cell proliferation, as demonstrated by cell growth and colony formation assays (Supplementary Fig. S4B–D), and enhanced cell migration capacity (Supplementary Fig. S5A–B), which was consistent with the results observed in the overexpression experiments.

## Methods

Ethical compliance
All research involving human participants complied with all relevant ethical regulations. The study protocol (YXLL-KY-2022(068)) was approved by the Institutional Review Board of the First Affiliated Hospital of Shandong First Medical University (Jinan, China). Written informed consent was obtained from all participants, and the study was conducted in accordance with the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki.

GWAS data
The GWAS data for gastric cancer in East Asian populations included 167,122 individuals, including 7,921 cases and 159,201 controls. Additionally, we obtained summary statistics for 95 phenotypes (including diseases, biomarkers, and medication usage) with case numbers greater than 3,000 from the 220 phenotypes available in the BBJ database 36. In BBJ, genotyping was conducted using Illumina arrays, and genotype imputation was performed using the 1000 Genomes Phase 3 reference panel combined with Japanese whole-genome sequencing data. Variants with an imputation of Rsq ≥ 0.7 were retained. Phenotypes were derived from curated medical records, ATC-coded medication data, and biomarker measurements, with appropriate outlier removal and medication-specific adjustments. A GWAS for binary traits employed SAIGE to account for sample relatedness and case‒control imbalance, whereas BOLT-LMM was used for quantitative traits with adjustments for age, sex, and principal components. A comprehensive overview of the included GWAS datasets from East Asian populations is provided in Supplementary Data 3. To validate our findings, we utilized two independent cohorts: the Korean Genome and Epidemiology Study (KoGES) cohort, comprising 378 gastric cancer cases and 71,920 controls of East Asian ancestry, and the Million Veteran Program (MVP) cohort, comprising 1,152 cases and 449,540 controls of predominantly European ancestry.

Global genetic correlation analysis
Genetic correlation (rg) between each pair of diseases or traits was assessed using LD score regression (LDSC) with GWAS summary statistics 37. The equation used in the LDSC was as follows: 𝑬[𝜷𝒋𝜸𝒋] = 𝑵𝒔𝒓𝒈𝒍𝒋 / 𝑴 + 𝑵𝟏𝑵𝟐𝒓𝒈𝒍𝒋 / 𝑴 √𝑵𝟏𝑵𝟐, where 𝛽𝑗 and 𝛾𝑗 represent the effect sizes of SNP j on the two traits being tested, 𝑁1 and 𝑁2 are the sample sizes for the two traits, 𝑁𝑠 is the number of overlapping samples between the two traits, r is the phenotypic correlation in the overlapping samples, and 𝑙𝑗 is the LD score. In line with the authors’ recommendations, we used the default LDSC regression weights and limited the analysis to SNPs with an MAF > 5% in the reference panel for estimation.

In this analysis, precalculated linkage disequilibrium scores for HapMap3 SNPs were utilized. These scores were derived from individuals of Asian ancestry from the 1000 Genomes Project. SNP markers with an imputation INFO score less than 0.9 were excluded from the analysis. LDSC was also employed to estimate the SNP-based heritability of the examined traits 37.

Cell type-specific enrichment of SNP heritability
Stratified LDSC (S-LDSC) was employed in this study to identify specific functional categories or cell types that significantly affect the heritability of the traits under investigation. The baseline v1.1 model, which contains 53 functional annotations, including gene regions, conserved elements, and regulatory features, was used as the reference in all S-LDSC analyses to account for known sources of heritability 38. The annotation data used in this analysis were obtained from the Roadmap project and included information on six chromatin marks (DHS, H3K27ac, H3K36me3, H3K4me1, H3K4me3, and H3K9ac) across a diverse set of 88 cell types or tissues. These annotations were subsequently used to partition the SNP heritability of each trait. Additionally, the cell type annotations were grouped into nine categories, namely, adipose, central nervous system (CNS), digestive system, cardiovascular, musculoskeletal and connective tissue, immune and blood, liver, pancreas, and others. We visualized the annotation-specific enrichment values using a colour-scaled heatmap generated by the ComplexHeatmap package (v2.12.1) in R 4.2.3. The hierarchical clustering of annotations was performed on the basis of Euclidean distance metrics with complete linkage agglomeration, implementing the default clustering algorithm (hclust) within the ComplexHeatmap framework.

Multitrait analysis of GWAS (MTAG)
MTAG was employed to explore the genetic associations between gastric cancer and each of the other phenotypes separately by leveraging combined GWAS summary statistics from gastric cancer and one additional trait in each analysis 10. This approach enhances the ability to detect genetic loci associated with correlated traits by addressing sample overlap and incomplete genetic correlation. For the MTAG analysis, we used default parameters, including a genetic correlation prior of N (0,1), and applied cross-trait LD score regression intercepts to account for residual sample overlap. In the initial step of MTAG, variants were filtered by excluding noncommon SNPs, duplicated SNPs, or those with strand ambiguity. The pairwise genetic correlation between traits was subsequently estimated using LDSC, and these estimates were then used to calibrate the variance‒covariance matrix of the random effect component. Following calibration, a random-effects meta-analysis was performed by MTAG to generate SNP-level summary statistics. The suggestive significance threshold (P < 0.01) in single-trait GWAS was selected to capture potentially meaningful associations while maintaining stringency, as these signals were further validated by genome-wide significance in multitrait analysis. Pleiotropic SNPs that achieved genome-wide significance (P< 5×10–8) in the multitrait analysis and suggestive significance (P< 0.01) in the single-trait GWAS were prioritized. The major histocompatibility complex (MHC) region was treated as one locus because of its complex LD structure.

Two-sample Mendelian Randomization
In the two-sample Mendelian randomization (MR) analysis, we implemented five widely recognized statistical methods: inverse-variance weighted (IVW), MR‒Egger, weighted median, simple mode, and weighted mode. The IVW method, which served as the primary analytical approach, was applied under a multiplicative random effects model to estimate the causal association between genetic predisposition to gastric cancer and cardiovascular-related risk factors identified through the LDSC. The IVW method assumes no intercept term and employs the inverse of the variance as weights to optimize model fitting. To address potential pleiotropic effects, sensitivity analyses were conducted using the MR‒Egger method 39, which incorporates a weighted linear regression framework to detect and adjust for horizontal pleiotropy among the instrumental variables (IVs). The results are reported as odds ratios (ORs) with corresponding 95% confidence intervals (CIs), and statistical significance was defined as P < 0.05. All MR analyses were executed using the TwoSampleMR package in R software (version 4.0.2), ensuring robust and reproducible causal inference 40.

Patients and tissue samples
Human tissue samples for this study were obtained from a prospective cohort of 46 patients who underwent radical gastrectomy at the First Affiliated Hospital of Shandong First Medical University (Jinan, China) in 2023. For each patient, paired samples of primary gastric cancer tissue and matched adjacent non-tumourous gastric mucosa were collected. The cohort included 33 male and 13 female patients. The genotypic distribution of the rs12814712 variant was as follows: AG genotype (9 males, 7 females) and GG genotype (24 males, 6 females). The participant age distribution is provided in Supplementary Table S2. Sex was determined according to hospital medical records. Although sex was not incorporated as a biological variable in the primary genetic association study design, all clinical data were sex-disaggregated in the source material.

Written informed consent was obtained from all participants for the use of their tissue samples and associated clinical data for research purposes. No financial compensation was provided. Following collection, genomic DNA and total RNA were extracted from portions of the tissue samples for downstream analyses. The original tissue samples were not completely consumed during this process. Residual tissue materials (aliquots and tissue blocks) were cryopreserved and permanently stored at –80 °C in the institutional biobank of the First Affiliated Hospital of Shandong First Medical University.

These deidentified biospecimens and associated clinical data remain available for academic validation and collaborative research. Access requests can be submitted with a scientifically justified proposal and completion of a material transfer agreement (MTA). All such requests should be directed to the corresponding author, Guangyong Zhang (guangyongzhang@hotmail.com), for review and facilitation.

PCR-Sanger sequencing of rs12814712
We collected 25 mg of cancer tissue from each of the 46 gastric cancer patients and extracted genomic DNA using the Ezup Column Animal Genomic DNA Purification Kit (B518251; Sangon Biotech, China). The extracted genomic DNA was amplified by PCR, and the PCR amplification primers for the rs12814712 locus were as follows: forward primer (5’ to 3’): TCATACTATGGGCAACTTGGCAC; reverse primer (5’ to 3’): CGGCAGCCCAGAACAGTAAA. The PCR reaction mix included the following components: 10x Taq buffer (with MgCl2), 10 µM dNTPs (mix), forward and reverse primers at 10 μM, 1 μl of template genomic DNA, 5 U/μl Taq DNA polymerase, and sterile water added to a final volume of 25 µL. After amplification, the PCR products were purified by agarose gel electrophoresis, and the sequence of the PCR amplification products was detected by Sanger sequencing.

Quantitative Real-Time PCR
Total RNA was extracted from frozen gastric cancer tissue or cell lines with TRIzol reagent (G3013; Servicebio, Wuhan, China). Single-strand complementary DNA (cDNA) was synthesized with a ReverTra Ace qPCR RT Kit (FSQ-101; TOYOBO Co., Ltd., Osaka, Japan). For quantitative real-time PCR, SYBR Green Real-time PCR Master Mix (QPK-201; TOYOBO Co., Ltd.) was used following the manufacturer’s instructions. The total PCR volume was 20 μl, containing 0.1 μl of each primer. The target-specific primers used were designed by Huada Gene (Shenzhen, China), and the specific sequences are listed in Supplementary Table S3.

Cell culture
The HEK293T, AGS, and MKN45 cell lines were obtained from Procell (Wuhan, China) and cultured in DMEM (for HEK293T), Ham's F-12K (for AGS), or RPMI-1640 (for MKN45) medium (all from Gibco, Carlsbad, CA, USA), each supplemented with 10% foetal bovine serum (FBS; Gibco) and 1% penicillin/streptomycin (Gibco). The cells were incubated at 37°C in 5% CO₂. The identity of all the cell lines was verified by short tandem repeat (STR) analysis, and the cell lines were routinely screened for mycoplasma contamination.

Plasmid Constructs
For luciferase assay-related plasmids, the 2001-bp genomic fragment containing the rs12814712 (G>A) site and 1000-bp flanking sequences was cloned and inserted into 1) the pGL3-promoter vector (E1761; Promega, Madison, WI, USA) to assess its potential enhancer-like activity and 2) the pmirGLO vector (E1330; Promega, Madison, WI, USA) to simulate its regulatory ability in a downstream context (fragment sequences are shown in Supplementary Data 4). The SV40 promoter sequence was used in these two plasmids to determine promoter function (Supplementary Fig. S3A-B).

For gene loss- and gain-of-function assays, plasmids were constructed by LST Biotech (Shandong Co., Ltd., Jinan, China). For gene knockdown experiments, short hairpin RNA (shRNA) sequences targeting NR2C1 and VEZT (Supplementary Table S4) were cloned and inserted into the pLKO.1-EGFP vector. For gene overexpression, the full-length coding sequences of NDUFA12, FGD6, NR2C1, and VEZT were cloned and inserted into the corresponding expression vectors. Information on the sequences and vectors is provided in Supplementary Table S5. The newly constructed plasmids generated in this study are available from the corresponding author upon reasonable request for academic research.

Luciferase Assays
HEK293T and AGS cells (1×10⁵/well) were taken in 96-well plates and were transfected after 18 h of incubation, pGL3 constructs were transfected with 0.1 μg test plasmid plus 0.01 μg pRL-TK plasmid, and pmirGLO constructs were transfected with test plasmid alone. Luciferase activity was measured using a Dual-Luciferase® Reporter Assay System kit (E1910; Promega, Madison, WI, USA): cells were lysed with 20 μL of PLB (15 min of RT shaking), after which firefly (luciferase assay reagent II) and Renilla (Stop & Glo) luminescence was sequentially measured. Relative activity was calculated as the Firefly/Renilla ratio. The experiments were repeated in triplicate.

Cell transfection
Cells were seeded in 6-well plates (5 × 105 cells/well) and incubated for 18 h. Then, overexpression plasmids for the indicated genes (NDUFA12, FGD6, NR2C1, and VEZT) and knockdown plasmids for the indicated genes (NR2C1 and VEZT) were transfected using Lipofectamine 2000 (11668030; Invitrogen, Carlsbad, CA, USA) and Opti-MEM™ I (31985062; Invitrogen, Carlsbad, CA, USA) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. After the cells were incubated for 8 h, the medium was replaced with Ham's F-12K (for AGS) or 1640 medium (for MKN45) supplemented with 10% FBS. The sequences of the shRNAs for NR2C1 and VEZT are listed in Supplementary Table S4.

Cellular viability assay
Approximately 24 hours after transfection, 5000 cells were seeded into 96-well plates. Cell viability was then evaluated at 0, 24, and 48 hours using the Cell Counting Kit-8 (CCK-8) assay (CK04, Dojindo Laboratories, Kumamoto, Japan), following the methods described previously 41. After a 2-hour incubation, cellular viability was assessed using a microplate reader, and the absorbance was measured at a wavelength of 450 nm.

EdU staining
In accordance with the manufacturer's instructions, cell proliferation was assessed using an EdU staining kit (C0071S; Beyotime, Shanghai, China). Cells (1 × 104) in each group were incubated with EdU buffer (10 μM) at 37°C for 2 hours. The supernatant was then discarded, and the cells were washed twice with PBS, followed by fixation with paraformaldehyde for 20 min. Afterwards, the mixture was incubated with freshly prepared cocktail buffer. To calculate the proportion of EdU-positive cells, the number of fluorescently stained cells was divided by the number of DAPI-stained cells. The nuclei were then stained with DAPI (C1006; Beyotime, Shanghai, China). The cells were observed and photographed under a fluorescence microscope. EdU was excited by light at a wavelength of 488 nm to emit green fluorescence, while DAPI was excited by light at a wavelength of 340 nm to emit blue fluorescence.

Colony formation assay
Twenty-four hours after transfection, the transfected gastric cancer cells (1 × 103) were seeded into 6-well plates. After an additional 14 days of culture, the cells were fixed and stained with 1% crystal violet (Solarbio, Beijing, China). After being stained with crystal violet for 20 min, the colonies formed were counted.

Transwell assay
Transwell assays were conducted to evaluate the migration and invasion of AGS and MKN45 cells. For the migration assay, cells (4 × 104) were suspended in serum-free medium (120 μL) and added to the upper chamber. Medium containing 10% FBS (750 μL) was added to the lower chamber to induce cell migration. The cells that migrated were washed three times with PBS, fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde for 30 minutes, and stained with 1% crystal violet. Images were observed at 100× magnification.

Wound healing assay
Cells (6 × 105) were cultured on 6-well plates. A pipette tip was subsequently used to scratch the bottom of the plate. Free cells were washed away with PBS buffer. The migration distance was observed at 0 h and 48 h.

Statistics & Reproducibility
The overall study design involved computational analysis of population-level genetic data (GWAS) followed by experimental validation in independent patient tissues and cell line models. No statistical method was used to predetermine sample size for the GWAS analyses, as these utilized all available data from the specified biobanks (BBJ, KoGES, MVP). The sample size for the patient tissue cohort (n=46) was based on availability during the study period. No data were excluded from the GWAS summary statistics analyses. For cellular and molecular experiments, sample sizes were determined on the basis of common practices in the field to ensure adequate power for detecting effects, and all experiments were performed with at least three biological replicates. The experiments were not randomized. The investigators were not blinded to allocation during the experiments or outcome assessment. Statistical analyses were conducted using SPSS software (version 22.0) and GraphPad Prism (version 8.0). Data from cellular and molecular experiments are presented as the mean ± standard deviation (SD). Group differences were evaluated using one-way ANOVA. Significance levels in the figures are denoted as follows: *P < 0.05, **P < 0.01, and ***P < 0.001. To control for multiple comparisons in the genome-wide analyses (genetic correlation via LDSC, S-LDSC, and Mendelian randomization), Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) correction was applied, with significance defined as PFDR < 0.05.

Data availability
The GWAS summary statistics data used in this study are available in the GWAS Catalogue under the accession codes summarized in Supplementary Data 3 [https://www.ebi.ac.uk/gwas/]. The individual-level genotype and gene expression data generated in this study are available under restricted access to protect patient privacy and comply with ethical regulations; access can be obtained by submitting a formal request to the corresponding author, Dr. Guangyong Zhang (guangyongzhang@hotmail.com), for academic, noncommercial research purposes, which will then be reviewed by the Ethics Committee of The First Affiliated Hospital of Shandong First Medical University. A completed data transfer agreement may be needed. The raw individual-level clinical data are protected and are not available because of data privacy laws. Source data are provided with this paper.

Code availability
We conducted our analyses using a variety of publicly available software tools. The computational environment consisted of Python (v2.7.18), Perl (v5.16.3), and R (v4.2.3). Genetic correlation analyses between gastric cancer and 95 traits were conducted using LDSC v1.0.1, with subsequent S-LDSC to evaluate cell type-specific SNP heritability enrichment. Bidirectional Mendelian randomization was implemented through the TwoSampleMR R package (v0.6.4). For the multitrait GWAS meta-analysis of gastric cancer and its 25 genetically correlated traits, we employed MTAG v1.0.8. The custom scripts used in this study are deposited in Zenodo and are publicly accessible at https://zenodo.org/records/18085131.
